PARTIES TO THE PROCEEDING
Petitioners are Cutberto Viramonte s, Christopher
Khaya, Firearms Policy Coalition, Inc., and Second
Amendment Foundation. Petitioners were plaintiffs in
the district court and plaintiffs-appellants in the court
of appeals.
Respondents are Cook County, Illinois, Toni
Preckwinkle, in her official capacity as County Board
President and Chief Executive Officer of Cook County,
and Thomas Dart, in his official capacity as Sheriff of
Cook County. Respondents were defendants in the
district court and defendants-appellees in the court of
appeals.
Respondent Eileen O’Neill Burke, in her official
capacity as State’s Attorney for Cook County, was
substituted as a defendant-appellee by the court of
appeals for Kimberly M. Foxx, who previously held the
position and was a defendant in the district court and
defendant-appellee in the court of appeals. See Order,
Viramontes v. County of Cook , No. 24 -1437 (7th Cir.
June 6, 2025), Dkt. 59.

INTRODUCTION
The Second Amendment secures the right to keep
and bear arms, but like other rights enshrined in our
Constitution, it is not absolute. The Framers did not
intend to permit the possession or use of “any weapon
whatsoever in any manner whatsoever and for
whatever purpose.” District of Columbia v. Heller ,
554 U.S. 570, 626 (2008).  This principle is deeply
rooted in our Nation’s history, which is replete with
common-sense regulations of weapons that are
exceptionally dangerous, lethal, and prone to misuse.
When weapons are introduced into society that have
the capability to  perpetrate some of our most tragic
and frightening crimes, from mass shootings to
assassination attempts, democratically elected
legislators are permitted to respond with appropriate
regulation.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. Factual and Legal Background
1. The AR-15’s Military Origin. In the late 1950s,
General William G. Wyman, the Commanding
General of the U.S. Continental Army Command,
determined, as part of the Cold War arms race, that
American soldiers needed lighter military rifles that
could fire rapidly, accurately, and were easy to control.
Dallas T. Durham, The M-16: Tradition, Innovation,
and Controversy, U.S. Army Command & Gen. Staff
Coll. (2021). He asked gun manufacturers to develop a
combat rifle that would meet these specifications and

2
penetrate a steel helmet and body armor at 500 yards.
JA55. The ArmaLite Corporation heeded the call,
creating a rifle with both semiautomatic and
automatic firing capability called the AR-15. Id.
Comprehensive testing of the weapon led the U.S.
military to conclude in 1962 that the AR-15 was
“superior in virtually all respects” to competing
military weapons. Advanced R sch. Projects Agency,
Field Test Report, AR -15 Armalite Rifle ( Aug. 20,
1962). By 1963, the U.S. military had purchased over
100,000 AR -15s, adopted it as a standard issue
military rifle, and gave it a military designation —the
M-16. JA55; see also Bianchi v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438,
454 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc).
When the AR-15 entered the civilian market, the
weapon was manufactured to fire only in semi -
automatic mode, making it the “civilian version” of the
M-16. Staples v. United States , 511 U.S. 600, 603
(1994). The primary difference between the AR-15 and
the M-16 is  the M -16’s capacity for automatic fire.
Otherwise, both weapons have the same performance
characteristics and share “the same core design,” “the
same patented operating system,” “the same
ammunition,” “the same effective range,” “the same
muzzle velocity,” and deliver “the same kinetic
energy.” Bevis v. City of Naperville , 85 F.4th 1175,
1195-96 (7th Cir. 2023); accord JA55-56.
Both weapons have combat-functional features, a
pistol grip that supports accuracy and fast reload, and
the ability to use a detachable 30 -round magazine to

3
facilitate prolonged firefights. Bianchi, 111 F.4th at
455. Both weapons can effectively fire at the exact
same rate in semiautomatic mode. E. Gregory
Wallace, “Assault Weapon” Lethality, 88 Tenn. L. Rev.
1, 21-22, 26 (2020); Dep’t of the Army, FM 3-22.9, Rifle
Marksmanship: M16-/M4-Series Weapons 2-1 (2008).
U.S. Army soldiers are instructed that
semiautomatic fire is “[t]he most important firing
technique during fast -moving, modern  combat,”
emphasizing that it is “surprising how devastatingly
accurate rapid semiautomatic fire can be.” Id. at 7-8,
7-9. The Army thereby advises soldiers that the best
version of the M -16 is functionally the AR -15. See id.
at 7-9, 7-13.
In combat, it is exceedingly rare to engage in fully
automatic firing. (Expert Report of Ryan Busse, App.
535, Capen v. Campbell , No. 24 -1061 (1st Cir.). One
decorated U.S. Navy SEAL who engaged in a decade
of combat, including the 2011 Osama bin Laden raid,
explained that he “‘[n]ever once fired full auto.’”
Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 456 (internal citation omitted).
For decades, the AR -15 was acknowledged for
what it was —a weapon of war —and advertisements
trumpeted that AR -15s were manufactured in the
same factory and on the same production line as the
world-famous M -16. Gordon L. Rottman et al.,  The
M16 37-38, 43 (2011).
By the 1980s, more gun dealers began selling the
AR-15 to the public. Implicitly referencing the AR -15

4
and other firearms with a military origin, the firearms
industry referred to them as assault rifles or assault
weapons. JA18. A 1981 publication is representative:

Guns & Ammo (July 1981).
As members of the public increasingly purchased
AR-15 platform weapons,  mass shootings that
resulted in numerous casualties also increased. In
1989, for example, a man fired 105 rounds from a
semiautomatic AK-47 style rifle at 300 school children
enjoying recess at Cleveland Elementary School,
leaving 5 dead and 31 injured in  just two minutes.
Nelson Kempsky et al., A Report to Att’y Gen. John K.

5
Van de Kamp on Patrick Edward Purdy and the
Cleveland School Killings  5, 8 (1989),
https://perma.cc/VQ68-VENR. In 1994, a former
airman killed 4 and wounded 23 people with an AK-47
at the Fairchild Air Force Base hospital. See An
Airman’s Revenge: 5 Minutes of Terror , N.Y. Times
(June 22, 1994).
Ownership of such weapons threatened public
safety in Cook County  as well . In 1992, 7 -year-old
Dantrell Davis was walking to school with his mother
when he was killed by a sniper  armed with an AR-15
who fired a .223 round from the 10th-floor window of
a high -rise apartment building in Chicago. The
shooter was aiming at someone in another building
approximately 350 yards away, but Dantrell was left
dead on the ground, blood pooling around his head, his
mother powerless to s ave him. See People v. Garrett ,
658 N.E. 2d 1216, 1218-20 (Ill. App. Ct. 1995).
The velocity of a bullet fired from an AR-15 creates
maximum injury potential, including fractured bones,
amputations, multiple surgeries, massive blood
transfusions, and ultimately, more casualties. JA13,
16; Cameron McWhirter & Zusha Elinson, American
Gun: The True Story of the AR15 67 (2023). The AR-15
fires a .223 caliber bullet at 3,200 feet per second,
ensuring that the bullet will go unstable  faster,
“fragment and mushroom ” inside the human body,
and create a large internal wound cavity . Nat’l Ass’n
for Gun Rts. v. Lamont, 153 F.4th 213, 239-40 (2d Cir.
2025) (internal citation and quotation marks omitted).

6
AR-15s “were designed to achieve a simple goal:
fire a lot of bullets fast to kill or maim as many enemy
soldiers as possible.” McWhirter & Elinson, supra, at
41. Although the weapon constitutes (at most) 3-5% of
firearms in civilian circulation, see JA20, it is used in
25% of mass shootings that involve at least four
fatalities, see Bianchi, 111 F.4th at 456.
Studies have estimated that AR -15s have been
used to kill 13 -20% of police officers who died in the
line of duty. Id. at 457-58. Standard issue soft armor
worn by most police officers will not protect them from
a .223 round. Even when an officer is wearing hard
armor (which is exceptionally heavy, significantly
impairs mobility, and is cost -prohibitive), it only
protects the officer’s chest and back. Officers are at
substantial risk of death if they are struck by AR-15
gunfire anywhere else. Id.; JA43.
2. Cook County’s Ordinance and Other Similar
Regulations. Cook County is the second-largest county
in the country and is home to over five million people.
It includes Chicago and 133 other municipalities.
Every day, there are festivals, concerts, sporting
events, community gatherings and large family
backyard parties that are susceptible to mass casualty
scenarios. The AR-15’s ability to travel through doors
and walls coupled with its long -range lethality puts
Cook County’s citizens at risk.
In 1993, Cook County, like other jurisdictions,
responded to this risk by enacting assault weapons
regulations. See Cook County Ordinance No. 93-O-37;

7
see also 1989 Cal. Stat. ch. 19 ; 1990 N.J. Sess. Law
Serv. ch. 32 ; 1993 Conn. Pub. Act s 93-306; Daniel
Abrams, Ending the Other Arms Race: An Argument
for a Ban on Assault Weapons, 10 Yale L. & Pol’y Rev.
488, 489 & n.12 (1992) (citing Richard Tapscott,
Schaefer Lobbies Governors for U.S. Ban on Assault
Weapons, Wash. Post (Aug. 18, 1991 )). The County
recognized that assault weapons are “military style”
firearms with unique capability for use in crime, a
particular threat in a jurisdiction that already
struggled with gun violence. Cook County Ordinance
No. 93-O-37. In addition to posing an immense threat
to police officers, Cook County recognized that ready
access to assault weapons presented an acute threat
to public safety. Id.
Congress shared these concerns, and a year later,
enacted a federal assault weapons ban as part of the
Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of
1994. See Pub. L. No. 103 -322, § 110102, 108 Stat.
1796, 1996 -98 (1994). Three U.S. Presidents urged
this enactment, citing the problem of mass shootings.
Ltr. from Gerald R. Ford, Jimmy Carter, and Ronald
Reagan to Members of the U.S. House of
Representatives (May 3, 1994). This law was in effect
until it expired by its terms in 2004. See 108 Stat. at
2000.
Cook County then amended its law to include
firearms encompassed by the features -based test in
the federal ban. Cook County Ordinance No. 06-O-50.
The Ordinance was renamed the “Blair Holt Assault

8
Weapons Ban” to honor a Chicago high school student
who was killed while protecting his friend after a
gunman opened fire on a public transit bus. In 2013,
the Ordinance was again amended to update the list
of prohibited weapons and increase penalties. Cook
County Ordinance No. 13 -O-32. Today, the ban is
codified in the County’s Code of Ordinances, at
Sections 54 -210 through 215 (all together, the
“Ordinance”).
The Ordinance is limited to “assault weapons”
that are strictly defined as “semiautomatic rifle[s]”
able to accept a detachable large capacity magazine
and one or more of certain military -style features,
such as a folding or telescoping stock, a pistol gri p
without a stock, a barrel shroud, or a muzzle brake.
Cook County, Ill., Code of Ordinances §§  54-211, 54-
212. The Ordinance makes it unlawful to
“manufacture, sell, offer or display for sale, give, lend,
transfer ownership of, acquire, carry or possess any
assault weapon.” Id. § 54-212(a). Specific firearms are
outlawed under the Ordinance, including the “AK-47,”
“AR-15,” “Bushmaster XM15,” “Bushmaster Carbon
15,” “Bushmaster MOE series,” “ArmaLite M15,”
“Armalite M15-T,” and “Olympic Arms PCR.” Id. § 54-
211(7) (hereafter AR-15 platform weapons).
The Ordinance exempts law enforcement officers,
members of the armed forces, government employees,
and persons “transporting an assault weapon
firearm...while engaged in interstate travel.” Id. § 54-
212(a), 214(b). Firearms that are antique, inoperable,

9
and designed for Olympic target shooting events are
not covered by the Ordinance. Id. § 54-211. Persons
violating the Ordinance are subject to a fine between
$5,000.00 and $10,000.00 and may be sentenced to a
maximum of six months’ imprisonment. Id. § 54-
214(a).
Cook County is one of many state governments
that ban AR-15 platform  weapons, including
California, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland,
Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island,
Virginia, and Washington. 0F

At common law, English Parliament enacted

lawful purposes” in sufficient numbers, “it is
impossible to conclude that the people have
determined the arm is so dangerous it is unfit for use
by ordinary citizens.” Id. at 39. This theory misreads
this Court’s precedent.
Once it is established that a regulation pursues a
legitimate public safety objective in a permissible

constitutional validity.” Id.
3. Numbers alone cannot determine
constitutionality.  Otherwise, MCDs that turn AR-15
platform weapons into machineguns could be legalized

50
today because statistics reflect that their popularity
has risen significantly.
Moreover, a “common use” test that turns solely
on the sheer number of firearms possessed by the
populace poses serious administrability problems and
presents significantly more questions than answers.
Exactly what raw number or percentage of the country
would suffice to establish immunity from regulation
on common -use grounds ? How many state (or local)
laws are needed to demonstrate a “traditional
legislative practice”? How does this approach reconcile
with the general principle that  questions concerning
the constitutionality of one state’s law  cannot be
“answered by cataloging the practices of other States”?
Martin v. Ohio, 480 U.S. 228, 236 (1987).
Next, at what point in time should courts assess
numbers regarding the extent of a firearm’s
popularity? Petitioners seem to assume that the
counting should start whenever a litigant decides to
challenge the regulation, but their position is
misguided. By Petitioners’ logic, the constitutionality
of a ban could fluctuate from year to year depending
on the purchasing whims of consumers and the
manufacturing decisions of gunmakers.
Colt only produced roughly 2,400 AR-15s in 1964
and never made more than 5,000 annually until 1973.
McWhirter & Elinson , supra, at 153-54. Applying
Petitioners’ common use methodology, the AR -15
could have been constitutionally restricted when
civilian ownership was lacking but would be immune

51
from regulation after the federal ban was lifted and
sales increased. This would mean that if laws had
been passed in 1964 to ban the sale of AR-15s they
would be constitutional, but later identical laws would
not pass muster.  Petitioners do not address these
questions or gaps in logic , and history offers no
answers, because the Second Amendment has never
precluded regulation based on a firearm’s popularity
alone.
Legislatures should be slow to regulate and
willing to objectively assess the impact of a weapon on
public safety. But once it becomes clear that a new
weapon poses an unacceptable threat to human life,
legislatures should be able to act.  Under our “federal
structure,” states and localities can “compet[e] for
[the] mobile citizenry” with different approaches to
unusually dangerous weapons. Bond v. United States,
564 U.S. 211, 221 (2011) (quoting Gregory v. Ashcroft,
501 U.S. 452, 458 (1991)). And as Petitioners  point
out, many states in fact take a different view of the se
various policy arguments . Individuals who would
prefer to live where unusually dangerous weapons are
legal can “vote with their feet and move to a
jurisdiction where their views have prevailed. ”
Schoenthal v. Raoul , 150 F.4th 889, 920 (7th Cir.
2025), cert. denied, 146 S. Ct. 2158 (2026).

Purpose That Immunizes Them from
Regulation.
Even if common use could defeat an otherwise
sound regulation, such use would have to turn, not on
raw ownership numbers , but on the extent and
suitability for constitutionally protected uses. And
here, AR -15 platform weapons are not customarily
used for lawful self -defense or hunting  (to the extent
that hunting is a legitimate Second Amendment
concern).

1. It is well settled that self-defense is the Second
Amendment’s “‘central’ concern.” Wolford, 609 U.S. at
192 (quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 577 , 581, 599, 628,
635). The concept of self -preservation is a
fundamental value worthy of protection in the Bill of
Rights. Blackstone, for instance, described the arms
provision of the English Bill of Rights as safeguarding
“the natural right of resistance and self-preservation.”
Heller, 554 U.S. at 593 -94. And this Court has long
presumed that an inherent constitutional right to selfdefense exists. See, e.g. , Martin, 480 U.S. at 236.
Consequently, this Court in Bruen explained that the
Second Amendment covers firearms “‘in common use’
today for self-defense.” 597 U.S. at 32 (quoting Heller,
554 U.S. at 627).
However, as discussed supra at 36-38, AR -15
platform weapon s are not commonly used for self -
defense. Petitioners point to  surveys showing that
some people tell pollsters they purchase AR -15s for
that purpose , Petrs. Br. 11 -12, but a survey
participant’s articulated intent is not dispositive of
constitutional questions . See e.g ., Counterman v.
Colorado, 600  U.S. 66, 74 -77 (2023)  (subjective
intentions alone are not determinative of categories of
speech that are carved out of the First Amendment).
Indeed, “constitutional rights are generally not
defined by the subjective intent of those asserting the
rights. The problems inherent in such a standard are
self-evident.” Hudson v. Palmer, 468 U.S. 517, 525 n.7
(1984). Among other things, the “general preference of

54
constitutional law for objective inquiries over
subjective ones” “spare[s] courts the practical
difficulties of assessing the sincerity and
idiosyncrasies of individual litigants.” Elhady v.
Kable, 993 F.3d 208, 222 (4th Cir. 2021) (citing Whren
v. United States, 517 U.S. 806, 813-14 (1996)).
To the extent that any “common use” inquiry falls
within step two of the Second Amendment’s governing
framework, the AR-15 is not a  suitable firearm for
self-defense and is not customarily used for that
purpose.
2. The Solicitor General contends that the Second
Amendment protects arms commonly owned for
hunting, and that AR-15 platform weapons are
commonly used for that purpose. U.S. Amicus Br. 26.
Petitioners, however, acknowledge that the AR -15 is
not suitable for all hunting, particularly, anything
larger than varmint. Petrs. Br. 9.
This Court has suggested that hunting for
“sustenance” is a lawful purpose. Wolford, 609 U.S. at
193 n.4.  But “ assault rifles were not designed for
traditional hunting,” and “[n]either was the .223
caliber / 5.56mm cartridge.” Expert Report of  James
Yurgealitis 27, Viramontes v. Cook County, No. 21-cv-
4595 (N.D. Ill.), Dkt. 81-5. Rifles designed for hunting
“traditionally have an internal magazine capacity of
less than 10 rounds depending on caliber.” Id. at 26.
“Most traditional hunting rifles or sporting rifles . . .
do not have the ability to accept” or “use detachable
magazines with varying capacities .” Yurgealitis Tr.

“Assault rifles were designed for fighting wars,” not

Today, of course, these responsibilities are
reserved for the United States military, which
maintains trained professional armies across the
globe. Certainly, this marks a dramatic shift from the
founding, when there was a deep mistrust of standing
armies, and colonists rightly feared the British
soldiers quartered amongst them. See Quartering Act
1774, 14 Geo. 3 c. 54 (Gr. Brit.) . But cf. U.S. Const.
amend. III.
But the founders wisely struck a balance between
the citizen -militia and the professional army , U.S.
Const. art. I, § 8; cf. U.S. Const. amend. II-III, which
allowed the fledgling nation to pragmatically reassess
its view of national and domestic security “when new
political, economic, technological, and strategic
realities necessitated an abandonment of revered, but
outmoded, military practices.”  William S. Fields &
David T. Hardy, The Militia and the Constitution: A
Legal History, 136 Mil. L. Rev. 1, 42 (1992).
This Court in Heller acknowledged the inevitable
tension forged at the intersection of technological
advancement and societal change:
Indeed, it may be true that no amount of
small arms could be useful against
modern-day bombers and tanks.  But the

57
fact that modern developments have
limited the degree of fit between the
prefatory clause and the protected right
cannot change our interpretation of the
right.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 627-28.
Thus, while a law-abiding citizen might well claim
that a machinegun is useful for repelling invasions,
suppressing insurrections, and resisting tyranny, and
may wish to train with the weapon for those purposes,
this Court has recognized the lawfulness of the federal
ban on machineguns irrespective of these purposes or
their degree of use. See id. So too with regard to hand
grenades, rocket launchers, and any number of other
unusually dangerous weapons.
Undoubtedly, some Americans may enjoy owning
AR-15s for use in  target practice  and other
recreational activities.8F
9 But the Constitution
generally leaves it to elected representatives to decide
when enjoyable but dangerous products may be sold to
the public. And the Second Amendment does not
dictate otherwise for a militaristic weapon that is
excessively dangerous and ill-suited for self-defense or
hunting.
